docs.description: Case name: Washington v. Texas Opinion filed: 1967-06-12 Docket No.: 649 Citations: • 18 L. Ed. 2d 1019 • 87 S. Ct. 1920 • 388 U.S. 14 • 1967 U.S. LEXIS 1083 Case holding summaries: • holding that Texas state statute prohibiting persons charged or convicted as co-conspirators in the same crime from testifying for one another arbitrarily violated the accused's right to put witnesses on the stand as well as compel their attendance in court • "It is undisputed that [the proffered] testimony would have been relevant and material . . . ." • striking a Texas statute which foreclosed defense testimony from a coparticipant in a crime • striking down Texas statute prohibiting testimony of defendant's alleged accomplice • “The Framers of the Constitution did not intend [in the Sixth Amendment] to commit the futile act of giving to a defendant the right to secure the attendance of witnesses whose testimony he had no right to use.” • “The right to offer the testimony of witnesses, and to compel their attendance, if necessary, is in plain terms the right to present a defense . . . .” • “The absurdity of the rule is amply demonstrated by the exceptions that have been made to it” • rule excluding accomplice testimony “prevent[s] whole categories of de fense witnesses from testifying on the basis of a priori categories that presume them unworthy of belief” • holding that due process requires the defendant to be given reasonable notice of the charges against him and an opportunity to be heard in his defense, which includes the rights listed in Chambers • discussing right to compulsory process for obtaining witnesses under the Sixth Amendment • "The right to offer the testimony of witnesses . . . is in plain terms the right to present a defense, the right to present the defendant's version of the facts as well as the prosecution's to the jury so it may decide where the truth lies." • “Just as an accused has the right to confront the prosecution’s witnesses for the purposes of challenging their testimony, he has the right to present his own witnesses to establish a defense. This right is a fundamental element of due process of law.” • recognizing defendant’s right to present his version of the facts to jury so it may decide where truth lies • indicating that "the right to present a defense" is a "fundamental element of due process of law" • applying this right to state trials • indicating that “the right to present a defense” is a “fundamental element of due process of law” • striking down Texas statute prohibiting testimony of defendant's alleged accomplice • because Texas law permitted accomplice to testify in situations presenting strong incentive to commit perjury, Texas could not preclude accomplice from testifying on behalf of defendant • discussing the right to offer witness testimony to the 11884 CUDJO v. AYERS jury • "The right of an accused to have compulsory process for obtaining witnesses in his favor stands on no lesser footing than the other Sixth Amendment rights that we have previously held applicable to the States." • 6th Amendment violation occurs when defendant is arbitrarily deprived of 'testimony ... relevant and material, ... and vital to the defense.' • invalidating state evidence rule declaring accomplices to be "incompetent" as witnesses unless they were testifying for the prosecution or had been acquitted • recognizing compulsory process right in state- defendants to possibly exculpating testimony of third persons despite state-law privilege against disclosure • "The right to offer the testimony of witnesses . . . is in plain terms the right to present a defense . . ." • identifying compulsory process right as fundamental and incorporating it into the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause • noting that a defendant's "right to present his own wit- nesses to establish a defense . . . is a fundamental element of due pro- cess of law" • invalidating state evidence rule declaring accomplices to be "incompetent" as witnesses unless they were testifying for the prosecution or had been acquitted • denial of right to present vital evidence of a co-defendant • holding that the Sixth Amendment right to present one's own witnesses as part of one's defense is a "fundamental element of due process" • a state statute that barred testimony of a coparticipant in a crime when offered by defendants as exculpatory evidence, but allowed as evidence for the prosecution, denied the defendant his right to compulsory process • explaining that the right to compulsory process would be meaningless if the defendant lacked the right to use the witnesses whose presence he compelled • Sixth Amendment was violated by a state statute which disqualified persons charged as principals, accomplices or accessories in the same crime from testifying in behalf of one another, while permitting such persons to testify in behalf of the prosecution • describing the rights guaranteed under the due process clause, including, inter alia, the right to present a defense and the right "to present the defendant's version of the facts as well as the prosecution's to the jury so it may decide where the truth lies" • invalidating state evidence rule declaring accomplices to be "incompetent" as witnesses unless they were testifying for the prosecution or had been acquitted • rule could not be rationally defended • holding that the federal compulsory process clause is incorporated in the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment • defendant has right to offer testimony of witnesses to establish a defense and truth is more easily ascertained when court allows relevant testimony to be admitted, leaving the weight of such testimony to be determined by fact-finder • "It is undisputed that [the proffered] testimony would have been relevant and material...." • a State cannot arbitrarily bar "whole categories of defense witnesses from testifying" • “The right to offer the testimony of witnesses, and to compel their attendance, if necessary, is in plain terms the right to present a defense, the right to present the defendant's version of the facts as well as the prosecution’s to the jury so it may decide where the truth lies.” • invalidating state evidence rule declaring accomplices to be "incompetent" as witnesses unless they were testifying for the prosecution or had been acquitted • indicating that "the right to present a defense" is a "fundamental element of due process of law" • rule barring co-conspirators from testifying • "The right to offer the testimony of witnesses, and to compel their attendance, if necessary, is in plain terms the right to present a defense." • "The right to offer the testimony of witnesses, and to compel their attendance, if necessary, is in plain terms the right to present a defense.... This right is a fundamental element of due process of law." • holding that a state statute that prohibited the defendant from calling a witness who had been charged and previously convicted of committing the same murder is unconstitutional • striking down Texas statute prohibiting testimony of defendant’s alleged accomplice • right to present witnesses to establish defense is fundamental to due process • applying the Compulsory Process Clause to defeat a state evidence rule, but noting that "[n]othing in this opinion should be construed as disapproving testimonial privileges . . ." • rejecting the federal rule that co-defendants were only competent witnesses for the state

docs.description: Case name: Norfolk & Western R. Co. v. Ayers Opinion filed: 2003-03-10 Docket No.: 01-963 Citations: • 155 L. Ed. 2d 261 • 123 S. Ct. 1210 • 538 U.S. 135 • 2003 U.S. LEXIS 1956 Case holding summaries: • "FELA renders common carrier railroads liable in damages to any person suffering injury while ... employed by [the] carrier if the injury or death result[ed] in whole or in part from the [carrier's] negligence." • fear of bladder cancer from "benzidine test" on prisoner to detect blood on skin • "It would be particularly curious for Congress to refer expressly to the established principle of comparative negligence, yet say not a word about adopting a new rule limiting the liability of the [defendant] on the basis of [another party's] negligence." • joint and several liability remains the rule in admiralty • "State laws are not controlling in determining what the incidents of this federal right shall be" • plaintiff asserting noncancer asbestos claims may not recover any cancer-related damages • sustaining jury charge allowing fear of cancer damages for plaintiff with "confirmed asbestosis" • "The cost of human injury, an inescapable expense of railroading, must be borne by someone, and the FELA seeks to adjust that expense equitably between the worker and the carrier." • predecessor statute declared unconstitutional because it regulated employee injuries not sufficiently related to interstate commerce • sustaining a verdict including fear-of-cancer damages where trial judge found plaintiff "ha[d] a genuine, real believable fear of cancer" (internal quotation marks omitted) • FELA decision holding erroneous "Trial Court's exclusion of evidence about [asbestosis claimant's] fear of cancer" • occupational diseases caused by exposure to hazardous dusts are injuries under the FELA • claim for fear of future disease held "clearly cognizable where, as here, plaintiff's exposure to asbestos has resulted in physical injury" • fear of deterioration of hip bone following motor vehicle accident • fear of cancer from ingestion of contaminated well water • fear of cancer compensable, but plaintiff established cancer more likely than not to occur • fear that brain injury from motor vehicle accident would lead to epilepsy • fear of a recurrence of cancer when first cancer was untimely diagnosed as a result of medical malpractice • railroad sued by employee under the FELA filed a third-party complaint against another party • fear of illness from drinking contaminated well water • toxic chemical spilled on hand • denying fear-of-cancer damages to asbestosis claimant based in part on misplaced reliance on Metro-North Commuter R. Co. v. Buckley, 521 U. S. 424 (1997) • sustaining award of damages that included compensation for asbestosis claimant's fear of cancer • asbestosis claimants, who suffered "substantial bodily harm" from asbestos, may recover for fear of cancer • apprehension of blood poisoning from foot injury • "general concern for [one's] future health" held insufficient to support recovery for an asbestosis sufferer's fear of cancer • sustaining jury charge allowing damages for asbestosis claimants' fear of cancer • "[T]he inquiry in these cases today rarely presents more than the single question whether negligence of the employer played any part, however small, in the injury or death which is the subject of the suit." • recovery permissible under the FELA only on showing that plaintiff will probably develop cancer from asbestos exposure • "Where both the physical injury and the nervous shock are proximately caused by the same act of negligence, there is no necessity that the shock result exclusively from the physical injury." • "Thus, damages for mental anguish concerning the chance that a future disease or condition will result from an original injury are generally not recoverable where the connection between the anxiety and the existing injury is too remote or tenuous" • noting that Gottshall relied upon cases involving "a threatened physical contact that caused, or might have caused, immediate traumatic harm" • denying fear-of-cancer recovery where condition "causes emotional distress only because the worker learns that he may become ill after a substantial period of time" • "The common law permits emotional distress recovery for that category of plaintiffs who suffer from a disease." • "emotional distress damages sought by asbestosis-afflicted plaintiff" found to fit "within a category where the law already permitted recovery for mental distress" • "[C]ourts ... must consider the general impact ... of the general liability rules they ... create." • describing joint and several liability as "settled by innumerable authorities" and citing federal decisions from 1883, 1893, 1894, 1895, 1902, 1904, 1906, 1910, and 1913 • evidence of increased risk of cancer held "admissible to establish, as a damage factor, the reasonableness of [an asbestosis claimant's] fear that he would contract cancer" • "Once Congress has relied upon conditions that the courts have created, we are not as free as we would otherwise be to change them." • prejudgment interest is not available under the FELA because it was unavailable at common law when the statute was enacted • describing FELA's "central focus on physical perils" • defining negligently inflicted emotional distress as "mental or emotional harm (such as fright or anxiety) that is caused by the negligence of another and that is not directly brought about by a physical injury" • "[T]hese terms traditionally have been used to describe sensations stemming directly from a physical injury or condition" (internal quotation marks omitted) • cancer evidence held admissible to show reasonableness of asbestosis claimant's fear of cancer • “[I]t accords with the FELA’s overarching purpose to require the employer to bear the burden of identifying other responsible parties and demonstrating that some of the costs of the injury should be spread to them.” • "those who escaped instant physical harm, but were `within the zone of danger of physical impact'" • recovery allowed under "zone of danger" test for NIED where the plaintiff has been diagnosed with asbestosis, and damages for "fear of cancer" are alleged as part of the pain and suffering associated with existing asbestos-related disease • "Many courts in recent years have considered the question presented here whether an asbestosis claimant may be compensated for fear of cancer. Of decisions that address the issue, a clear majority sustain recovery." [citing Cox ] • "parasitic" generally defined as "associated with"
